authored_explainer.title: Cereal production Is 1.5x Higher Than In 1972
authored_explainer.hook: By the 1970s, experts warned the world would run out of food.
says: In 1985, progression to secondary school (%) was 77.8; by 2017, 91.3—1.2 times higher, meaning more students made the transition.
In 1972, cereal production was 1083.7 million metric tons; by 2024, 1644.1—1.5 times higher. The scarcity forecasts missed the mark.
Farmland covers 5.2 million square kilometers in China, 4.2 in the United States, 3.6 in Australia, 2.4 in Brazil, and 2.2 in Russia.
authored_explainer.closing: The famine everyone predicted never showed up—and that changes how we plan for scarcity.
authored_explainer.question: Which surprised you most—school, grain, or land?

authored_explainer.title: Combustible renewables and waste Is 3.0x Higher Than In 1990
authored_explainer.hook: One energy source tripled since 1990; it isn't solar or wind.
says: In 1990, combustible renewables and waste was 10.2 %; by 2024, 30.1 %—3.0 times higher. Waste-derived fuel remains a surprisingly large share.
In 1998, electricity access was 73.2 %; by 2024, 91.9 %—1.3 times higher.
In 1972, methane (ch4) emissions from waste were 903.8 Mt CO2e; by 2024, 1,652—1.8 times higher, revealing the climate tradeoff.
authored_explainer.closing: Waste can supply energy, but its methane cost still reaches everyone.
authored_explainer.question: Which surprised you most—fuel, power, or waste?

authored_explainer.title: Population growth Fell 54% Since 1972
authored_explainer.hook: Population growth was supposed to accelerate forever; the number proves it didn't.
says: In 1972, rural population was 63.1 %; by 2025, 42.2 %—down to 67 percent, as humanity shifted toward cities.
In 1972, population in the largest city was 18.2 %; by 2025, 16.2 %—barely moved, despite rapid urbanization.
In 1972, population growth was 2 annual %; by 2025, 0.91 annual %—down to 46 percent, transforming every long-term forecast.
authored_explainer.closing: The planet is still growing, but slower growth changes every plan built for endless acceleration.
authored_explainer.question: Which surprised you most—rural, city, or growth?
